ratings.plot: A young man and woman meet on a train in Europe, and wind up spending one evening together in Vienna. Unfortunately, both know that this will probably be their only night together.

verdict.reason: One of Linklater's essential films — a master class in dialogue and intimacy that demands the theater's full attention. Metrograph's restoration gives you the Vienna streets and faces in the clarity they deserve.

movies.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle

ratings.plot: Two unlike girls are going to learn each other's world - lovely countryside and bustling Paris.

verdict.reason: A Rohmer film about friendship and class collision belongs on the big screen, and this Metrograph restoration captures the precise social observation that makes his work essential. The four-part structure lets each encounter breathe—the kind of patient filmmaking that demands theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: A truck driver stops at a small family-run noodle shop and decides to help its fledgling business. The story is intertwined with various vignettes about the relationship of love and food.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest films about food and desire ever made—see it on a big screen where the anarchic energy and visual gags land hard. Itami's digressive structure and absurdist humor demand theatrical immediacy, and this DCP restoration at Metrograph gives the film's saturated colors and precise compositions the space they need.

movies.title: Days and Nights in the Forest

verdict.reason: Essential Ray on the big screen — this ranks among his finest character studies. The Metrograph restoration reveals the subtle interplay between natural light and psychological insight that makes his camera work irreplaceable.

movies.title: National Theatre Live: All My Sons (2026)

ratings.plot: America, 1947, Joe and Kate Keller are a success story. But their contented lives are about to shatter. A figure from the past forces long buried truths to the surface lying bare the price of their American dream.

verdict.reason: Jeremy Herrin's production of Miller's masterpiece is a rare chance to see one of the century's great moral reckonings on a screen built for it. The 165-minute runtime is earned by a cast working at full intensity in a play that demands nothing less than everything.

movies.title: How to Divorce During the War

ratings.plot: Set in Vilnius in 2022, high-flying executive Marija chooses the worst moment to discuss divorce with husband Vytas - one day before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The couple navigates separation amid a refugee crisis.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds emotional clarity in catastrophic timing, using a single marriage to frame the chaos of invasion. Blazevicius shoots Vilnius with the precision of a architect documenting a city about to break.

ratings.plot: When three American doctors-Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian-enter Gaza to save lives, they find themselves caught between medicine and politics, risking everything to expose the truth.

verdict.reason: A urgent documentary about doctors navigating impossible choices in an active crisis—this is the kind of film that demands a theater and the moment it's playing. Poh Si Teng's debut has the immediacy and moral weight that justify leaving home tonight.

ratings.plot: Biopic of 1930s Chinese actress Lingyu Ruan.

verdict.reason: Stanley Kwan's 1991 masterpiece about Lingyu Ruan uses fragmented narrative and layered performance to interrogate cinema, stardom, and historical truth itself. Film Forum's repertory screening of this restored print is essential viewing for anyone serious about film history or the power of biographical cinema.

ratings.plot: A group of professors working on a new encyclopedia while living in a Manhattan mansion take in a mouthy nightclub singer who is wanted by the police to help bring down her mob boss lover.

verdict.reason: Hawks' screwball masterpiece belongs on a theater screen, not your couch. Gary Cooper and Barbara Stanwyck generate enough electricity to power the whole city, and the rapid-fire dialogue demands full attention in a room full of people who'll laugh at the same moments you do.

ratings.plot: American professor John Holden arrives in London for a parapsychology conference, only to find himself investigating the mysterious actions of Devil-worshipper Julian Karswell.

verdict.reason: Tourneur's 1957 masterpiece of atmospheric dread belongs on the big screen where its shadow-work and mounting tension hit hardest. The restoration at Lincoln Center is the place to experience this film's command of mood and its rare balance of supernatural terror and intellectual rigor.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's purest expressions of moral urgency told through a child's journey—Kiarostami's mastery is in every frame. The 83 minutes moves with such clarity and grace that it plays like a parable, and the Alamo screenings offer the big screen this deserves.

ratings.plot: A troubled child summons the courage to help a friendly alien escape from Earth and return to his home planet.

verdict.reason: Essential big screen viewing for one of Spielberg's most emotionally direct films. John Williams' soaring theme and the bicycle chase finale demand theatrical sound and scale.

ratings.plot: When a newspaper editor's ace reporter ex-wife is about to quit her job and remarry, he buys himself time to win her back by promising her an exclusive interview with a death row convict.

verdict.reason: Hawks orchestrates overlapping dialogue at a pace that still feels urgent and alive, something few comedies manage even now. The speed and rhythm of the screenplay demand theatrical presence to land the jokes.

movies.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp

ratings.plot: A director making a slasher sequel becomes obsessed with casting the original film's 'final girl,' leading both women into psychological and sexual chaos.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's take on meta-horror and obsession demands the big screen and the 35mm print available at multiple venues. The film's formal control over tone and image—slipping between genres without losing grip—is a theatrical experience, not a home one.

ratings.plot: A self-conscious woman juggles adjusting to her new role as an aristocrat's wife and avoiding being intimidated by his first wife's spectral presence.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's only Best Picture winner holds up as a masterclass in psychological suspense and Gothic atmosphere on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the shadows and compositions that make this 1940 film feel as immediate as a modern thriller.

ratings.plot: Two teenagers share a profound, magical connection upon discovering they are swapping bodies. Things manage to become even more complicated when the boy and girl decide to meet in person.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return for one of anime's most beloved films—Shinkai's visual mastery and emotional precision demand the big screen. The animation detail and color grading will flatten on any smaller display.

ratings.plot: A counterfeit bill that starts off as a schoolboy prank leads to incarceration and violence.

verdict.reason: Bresson's final film is a masterpiece of moral devastation that demands the theater. The DCP restoration at Metrograph shows the crystalline austerity of his compositions and the accumulating weight of casual cruelty with devastating clarity.

ratings.plot: Nelly has just lost her grandmother and is helping her parents clean out her mother's childhood home. She explores the house and the surrounding woods. One day she meets a girl her age building a tree-house.

verdict.reason: Sciamma's shortest film is also her most direct statement about time, memory, and the people we become—see it on the big screen while you can. At 73 minutes, it respects your night and leaves you changed.

ratings.plot: The life of Mason, from early childhood to his arrival at college.

verdict.reason: Linklater's 12-year experiment in durational filmmaking remains essential viewing on the big screen. The real passage of time across the cast's faces and bodies cannot be replicated at home.

ratings.plot: Based on Honobu Yonezawa's novel. Set in 16th century Japan, follows Lord Murashige Araki who, besieged in his castle, confronts mysterious crimes and allies with imprisoned strategist Kanbei Kuroda to uncover the truth.

verdict.reason: Kurosawa returns with a 16th-century mystery that plays to his strengths in atmosphere and narrative layering. The combination of his direction, a literary source, and three major repertory venues makes this a rare theatrical event.

ratings.plot: Amziah King, beekeeper, musician, and anchor of his community, reunites with former foster daughter Kateri after many years apart, and fends off threats to his honey business.

verdict.reason: Andrew Patterson makes character-driven thrillers that work on the strength of performance and mood over plot mechanics, and this reunion story set around a honey business is exactly the kind of specific human drama that justifies a theater ticket. The 130-minute runtime lets the relationships breathe in ways that matter.

ratings.plot: Joe and Angela's marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places.

verdict.reason: Wilde directs a sharp ensemble comedy about marriage and desire with real bite and sexual tension. The dinner-party structure gives the night room to breathe and fracture in ways that feel both funny and genuinely unsettling.

ratings.plot: On lakeside summer holiday, a conflicted older man is dared to have a flirt with two beautiful teenage half-sisters despite his betrothal to a diplomat's daughter and the fact that the girls have boyfriends.

verdict.reason: Rohmer's masterpiece of desire and moral restraint deserves the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the precision of his compositions and the lake light that makes every conversation feel like it matters.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at peak visual invention deserves the big screen, and this neon-soaked crime film moves with a kinetic energy that streaming kills. Metrograph's DCP presentation restores the chromatic intensity that makes every frame feel like a deliberate painting.

ratings.plot: 24 hours in the lives of three young men in the French suburbs the day after a violent riot.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films about urban rage and class in cinema, and Metrograph's DCP restoration makes this the right place to see it. Kassovitz's black-and-white cinematography and the unflinching 98-minute sprint through a single day demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan on 70mm is a theatrical event worth the commitment to nearly three hours. The format choice across multiple venues means the image and sound were designed for the biggest screen in the room.

ratings.plot: After his family is murdered by a notorious and ruthless bandit, a former police officer enlists the services of two outlaws to capture the bandit.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's great action films—see it restored on a big screen at Metrograph. The DCP brings new life to Ramesh Sippy's 1975 masterpiece of wit, violence, and friendship that shaped Hindi cinema for decades.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A restrained zombie film that uses genre mechanics to examine human selfishness under pressure—rare enough to justify the trip. The restoration at IFC Center sharpens the kinetic train-set staging that made this work in the first place.

ratings.plot: Vietnam War's first Black special ops team reunites to share their untold story, revealing hidden military history and exploring whether confronting the past can heal old wounds.

verdict.reason: Watch this. A firsthand account of an erased chapter of military history—the kind of documentary that restores what official channels buried.

ratings.plot: A documentary about writer and director Brian De Palma.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone serious about cinema craft and narrative design. Baumbach and Paltrow let De Palma himself do the teaching, breaking down how he builds suspense and composes a frame with the precision of a surgeon.

ratings.plot: Two boys begin a silence strike to press their parents into buying them a television set.

verdict.reason: One of Ozu's masterpieces about Japanese family life, rendered in color for the first time in this restoration. The deadpan humor and formal compositions make this a rare theatrical event that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: Baron "Bear" Bailey breaks a novelty charm to force his co-worker Nikki Freeman to love him, but the supernatural compulsion warps her mind into violent obsession, trapping him in a nightmare he cannot wish away.

verdict.reason: A high-concept supernatural thriller that weaponizes wish-fulfillment into genuine horror, executed with enough craft to justify the runtime. Metrograph's DCP presentation will render the warped visual language of compulsion and psychological unraveling with the clarity it demands.

ratings.plot: When a menace known as the Joker wreaks havoc and chaos on the people of Gotham, Batman, James Gordon and Harvey Dent must work together to put an end to the madness.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print, which is the only way to see Nolan's compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: After a threat from the tiger Shere Khan forces him to flee the jungle, a man-cub named Mowgli embarks on a journey of self discovery with the help of panther Bagheera and free-spirited bear Baloo.

verdict.reason: Favreau's photorealistic animation remains a technical marvel that demands the theatrical image. Metrograph's 35mm print is the ideal way to see the jungle rendered at this scale and clarity.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Iosseliani's debut in a restored DCP at Metrograph. The film's gentle comedy and kinetic street-level observation of Tbilisi justify the trip for anyone interested in Soviet-era cinema outside the monumental tradition.

ratings.plot: A former San Francisco police detective juggles wrestling with his personal demons and becoming obsessed with the hauntingly beautiful woman he has been hired to trail, who may be deeply disturbed.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's greatest achievements belongs on the big screen, and this 35mm print at Metrograph is the way to experience Hitchcock's command of color, space, and visual obsession. The vertigo effect and San Francisco locations demand theatrical scale to hit their full hypnotic power.

movies.title: Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown

ratings.plot: A television actress encounters a variety of eccentric characters after embarking on a journey to discover why her lover abruptly left her.

verdict.reason: Essential Almodóvar at peak invention, vital in 35mm. The 88-minute runtime moves like a perfectly wound toy, and Metrograph's print restores the saturated color palette that makes every frame feel like a poster.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Matt Johnson captures the specific texture of a kitchen summer in 1985 with the precision of someone who understands how small moments calcify into a life.

ratings.plot: Henry Graham lives the life of a playboy. When his lawyer tells him that his lifestyle has consumed all his funds, Henry must avoid climbing down the social ladder. He plans to marry wealthy scientist Henrietta Lowell - and kill her.

verdict.reason: Worth seeing for May's brilliant directorial debut, which she also wrote and starred in with perfect misanthropic timing. Her chemistry with Walter Matthau creates one of the sharpest dark comedies of the 1970s.

ratings.plot: Carrie White, a shy, friendless teenage girl who is sheltered by her domineering, religious mother, unleashes her telekinetic powers after being humiliated by her classmates at her senior prom.

verdict.reason: De Palma's debut is essential viewing on a big screen, where the precision of his split-screens and the shower sequence's sustained dread hit hardest. Sissy Spacek's performance captures a vulnerability that makes the final act devastation feel earned rather than exploitative.

ratings.plot: In Detroit, a pop-culture enthusiast steals cocaine from his new wife's pimp and tries to sell it in Hollywood, prompting the mobsters who own the drugs to pursue the couple.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's greatest film—a pulp romance that moves with genuine velocity and heartbreak. The Metrograph screening gives you the color saturation and kinetic editing that define Scott's visual language.

ratings.plot: A filmmaking family finds themselves in a real-life horror movie when a body turns up on the set of their low-budget slasher, forcing them to cover up the murder to keep filming.

verdict.reason: A clever genre hybrid that earns its setup—the collision of real violence and movie artifice generates genuine tension and dark comedy. The 81-minute runtime keeps the premise sharp instead of letting it overstay, and Lincoln Center's theatrical presentation honors the film's visual wit.

ratings.plot: Two 12-year-olds, who live on an island, fall in love with each other and elope into the wilderness. While people set out on a search mission, a violent storm approaching them catches their attention.

verdict.reason: Anderson's most purely joyful film deserves the big screen, and 94 minutes means no endurance test. The composition, color, and symmetry reward theatrical projection in ways streaming cannot touch.

ratings.plot: When greedy tycoons refuse to return Mothra's egg to the people of Infant Island, they must decide if they are willing to answer Japan's own pleas for help when Godzilla arises near Nagoya.

verdict.reason: This is peak Toho kaiju craft from Honda at his most confident, balancing spectacle with genuine visual wit. The miniature work and suit choreography in the final battle remain thrilling on a big screen, and the film's satirical edge about corporate greed bites harder than most monster movies ever dare.

ratings.plot: Two neighbors form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses. However, they agree to keep their bond platonic so as not to commit similar wrongs.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the chromatic precision that defines his visual language. The film's emotional restraint and compositional density reveal themselves only in a theater.

ratings.plot: A young woman, studying to be a vet, develops a craving for human flesh.

verdict.reason: Ducournau's debut is a rare horror film that earns its extremity through formal precision and genuine artistic vision. Metrograph's DCP presentation showcases the film's composed cinematography and color work, which are essential to how the body horror lands.

ratings.plot: A psychologist is sent to a station orbiting a distant planet in order to discover what has caused the crew to go insane.

verdict.reason: Worth the trip for one of cinema's greatest meditations on memory and identity, shot with Tarkovsky's hypnotic command of space and time. Metrograph's DCP restoration honors the film's deliberate pacing and architectural cinematography on a proper screen.

ratings.plot: Anna, a shy 12-year-old girl, is sent to spend time with her aunt and uncle who live in the countryside, where she meets Marnie. The two become best friends. But Anna gradually discovers that Marnie is not quite who she appears to...

verdict.reason: Studio Ghibli's final feature is a delicate ghost story about loneliness and connection that demands the big screen. Yonebayashi's watercolor animation and the Metrograph's DCP projection bring out textures that would dissolve on a small display.

ratings.plot: Wealthy Sunny von Bülow lies brain-dead, husband Claus guilty of attempted murder; but he says he's innocent and hires Alan Dershowitz for his appeal.

verdict.reason: Watch it; Barbet Schroeder's control of tone—oscillating between courtroom procedure and psychological suspense—makes this a rarer kind of legal drama than the genre usually allows. Jeremy Irons' performance as Claus is a masterclass in ambiguity, refusing to tip the film's hand about guilt or innocence in ways that feel earned rather than manipulative.

ratings.plot: A Juilliard-trained violist navigates the New York City freelance classical musician scene, playing gigs that often draw her into the personal lives of strangers, all while living in her oddball family's NYC apartment.

verdict.reason: A sharp, funny film about the precarious life of a working musician in New York that finds real humanity in the gig economy and the people who sustain it. The 78-minute runtime and Hagen's observant direction let the film breathe without overstaying, and the Juilliard violist protagonist grounds the comedy in authentic detail.

ratings.plot: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime.

verdict.reason: Pixar's sequels rarely lose the thread, and this one expands the premise without abandoning what made the originals work. The animation team has spent five years perfecting how light hits plastic and felt, which matters on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: A lazy, irresponsible young clerk (Sir Tom Courtenay) in provincial Northern England lives in his own fantasy world and makes emotionally immature decisions as he alienates friends and family.

verdict.reason: A essential British New Wave film that holds up as sharp social comedy and genuine character study. Schlesinger's direction gives the fantasy sequences visual wit that makes Billy's escape from provincial life feel both comic and tragic.

ratings.plot: A nerdy florist finds his chance for success and romance with the help of a giant man-eating plant who demands to be fed.

verdict.reason: Go to Alamo Drafthouse; Frank Oz's musical comedy belongs in a theater where the fun can breathe. The songs and Rick Moranis's nervy charm demand a crowd.

ratings.plot: When Sebastian, a pianist, and Mia, an actress, follow their passion and achieve success in their respective fields, they find themselves torn between their love for each other and their careers.

verdict.reason: A musical that actually earns its sentiment through craft and performance rather than manipulation. Chazelle shoots Los Angeles like a living character, and the chemistry between Stone and Gosling carries you through all 128 minutes.

ratings.plot: Intent on seeing the Cahulawassee River before it's dammed and turned into a lake, outdoor fanatic Lewis Medlock takes his friends on a canoeing trip they'll never forget into the dangerous American back-country.

verdict.reason: One of the great survival films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Boorman's control of landscape and danger plays at full force. The river itself becomes the antagonist, and the print restores details in light and shadow that streaming flattens.

movies.title: The Night is Short Walk on Girl

ratings.plot: In this comedy about one epic night in Kyoto, a college sophomore goes on a series of surreal encounters with the local nightlife, all the while unaware of the romantic longings of her classmate Senpai.

verdict.reason: Yuasa's direction transforms a single night into a kaleidoscopic fever dream that demands the big screen and full sensory immersion. Metrograph's DCP projection will let you feel the hand-drawn chaos at full intensity.

ratings.plot: Ordinary word processor Paul Hackett experiences the worst night of his life after he agrees to visit Marcy, a Soho resident that he met that evening at a coffee shop.

verdict.reason: Scorsese's funniest film is a masterclass in escalating chaos and one of cinema's great fever dreams about the city turning hostile. The newly restored DCP at Metrograph sharpens the neon-soaked Manhattan nightmare that defined 1980s downtown cool.

ratings.plot: In a dystopian future, a group of students from a Japanese high school are forced by the government to compete in a battle, killing one another until only one is left standing.

verdict.reason: Fukasaku's final film is a savage, formally inventive work that demands the big screen—kinetic editing and visceral sound design collapse the distance between viewer and carnage. This is a rare theatrical revival of a banned-in-many-countries landmark that invented a genre; see it before it vanishes again.

ratings.plot: In the mid-19th century a mute woman is sent to New Zealand along with her young daughter and prized piano for an arranged marriage to a farmer, but is soon lusted after by a farm worker.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films of the 1990s demands to be seen on a theater screen, not streamed at home. Campion's control of image, sound, and performance—particularly Holly Hunter's wordless intensity—defines what cinema can do that no other medium can match.

ratings.plot: A cyborg from the future, identical to the one who failed to kill Sarah Connor, must now protect her ten-year-old son John from an even more advanced and powerful cyborg.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing on the biggest screen you can find. Cameron's practical effects work remains unmatched three decades later, and the T-1000's liquid metal transformations demand theatrical scale.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked romance is essential cinema on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP presentation brings the saturated colors and kinetic editing to full life.

ratings.plot: A writer recounts a childhood journey with his friends to find the body of a missing boy.

verdict.reason: One of the best American films about friendship and growing up—see it on the big screen. Metrograph's DCP restoration brings out the golden-hour cinematography and the texture of small-town Oregon in a way that matters for this film.

ratings.plot: A forgotten Peter Parker lives alone as a full-time Spider-Man until mounting pressure triggers a dangerous change and a powerful new enemy emerges.

verdict.reason: Destin Daniel Cretton has earned a theatrical ticket with his work on Shang-Chi, and this premise—Spider-Man stripped of his civilian life until everything breaks—is the most interesting angle the character has taken in years. IMAX is the format to choose here; the action design will justify the screen size.

ratings.plot: Arriving in Chicago, Henry moves in with ex-con acquaintance Otis and starts schooling him in the ways of the serial killer.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on a big screen—a landmark film about violence that refuses to aestheticize or exploit what it shows. McNaughton's deadpan direction and grainy 16mm stock make the brutality feel documentary-real in a way that home viewing completely loses.
A cult horror landmark that demands the big screen—Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see Lon Chaney Jr. and the film's twisted family dynamics with clarity they've never had before.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones makes films about art and obsession with the clarity of a poet himself, and this one earns its 90 minutes by letting each scene breathe. The Film Forum and Lincoln Center screenings matter because Jones's visual precision and the ensemble's intimacy need a room full of people paying attention.

ratings.plot: A movie sound recordist accidentally records the evidence that proves that a car accident was actually murder and consequently finds himself in danger.

verdict.reason: De Palma's best thriller, a masterwork of paranoid cinema that demands the big screen for its elaborate setpieces and sound design. The climax alone—a meticulously constructed sequence at the Liberty Day parade—justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: When a southern Italian town is rocked by a string of child murders, the police and two urban outcasts search for the culprit amid scapegoating within the superstitious community.

verdict.reason: Fulci's masterwork uses genre machinery to eviscerate mob justice and provincial cruelty with unflinching force. The 35mm print at Alamo Drafthouse is the right way to see a film this visually precise about the anatomy of blame.

ratings.plot: A woman starts exhibiting increasingly disturbing behavior after asking her husband for a divorce. Suspicions of infidelity soon give way to something much more sinister.

verdict.reason: Zulawski's 1981 masterwork of marital breakdown and body horror demands the big screen—this is cinema as pure psychological torment. Metrograph's restoration unlocks the film's hallucinatory intensity and makes the creature effects register with their full, nauseating power.

ratings.plot: Several women enter a science fiction author's life over the course of a few years, after the author has lost the woman he considers his one true love.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's most visually ambitious film demands a theater screen and Metrograph's DCP restoration lets the neon-soaked production design breathe. The 129-minute runtime tests patience, but the payoff is a rare work of sci-fi romance that uses visual style as narrative itself.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: This is a lean, tense thriller that works better than the sequels that buried its actual point about trauma and institutional cruelty. Sylvester Stallone's performance is genuinely affecting, and Ted Kotcheff keeps the action grounded in real geography and consequence for 93 minutes that don't waste a frame.

ratings.plot: A boy is left to his own devices when his mother refuses to pay for his schooling.

verdict.reason: A rare Eustache restoration at Metrograph—one of cinema's sharpest observations of childhood freedom and class constraint. The DCP brings new clarity to his deadpan mise-en-scène and the unsentimental comedy of a boy navigating Paris alone.

ratings.plot: Two city-bred siblings are stranded in the Australian Outback, where they learn to survive with the aid of an Aboriginal boy on his "walkabout": a ritual separation from his tribe.

verdict.reason: Roeg's visual command of the Outback is unmatched on small screens, and this 35mm print at Metrograph restores the color and light that define the film's language. The cinematography is the story.

ratings.plot: Amidst turmoil and racial conflict in a Francophone African state, a white French woman fights for her coffee crop, her family and ultimately for her life.

verdict.reason: Denis makes a film about colonial collapse that moves faster and hits harder than her reputation suggests. The final twenty minutes at Metrograph will stay with you.

Klapisch's 1996 debut is a rare theatrical screening of a film that captures the texture of youth and sibling friction with genuine affection. The 35mm print at Metrograph restores the grainy, lived-in look that defines the film's intimacy.

ratings.plot: Two pre-adolescent boys both experienced a strange event and later it affects their lives in different ways. One becomes a reckless, sexually adventurous prostitute, while the other retreats into a reclusive fantasy of alien abduc...

verdict.reason: Gregg Araki's unflinching direction and the restoration print justify the trip to see this film on a theater screen. The 105-minute runtime demands a committed viewing, and the restoration at IFC Center or Alamo Drafthouse reveals details that streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: While doing a thesis about violence, Ángela finds a snuff video where a girl is tortured until death. Soon she discovers that the girl was a former student in her faculty...

verdict.reason: Amenábar's debut is a taut thriller that earns its intellectual premise through genuine suspense and formal craft. The film builds dread through meticulous editing and sound design rather than cheap shocks, making this 1996 Spanish landmark worth seeing on a big screen at Lincoln Center.

ratings.plot: Three friends plan to pull off a simple robbery and go on the run.

verdict.reason: Anderson's debut is essential to understanding his career, and a rare theatrical showing of a film that defined his sensibility before it calcified into mannerism. The 91-minute runtime moves with actual momentum, something his later work abandoned.

ratings.plot: A young martial artist is caught between respecting his pacifist father's wishes or stopping a group of disrespectful foreigners from stealing precious artifacts.

verdict.reason: Jackie Chan at peak physical comedy—this is essential 90s action cinema that rewards the big screen. The drunken style choreography is intricate enough to demand theatrical clarity, and Chan's willingness to wreck his body for a gag plays best when you can see every impact.

ratings.plot: A couple take a trip to Argentina but both men find their lives drifting apart in opposite directions.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at his visual peak—worth the trip for a masterwork of color, movement, and heartbreak on the big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph lets you see every saturated frame and tracking shot as intended.

ratings.plot: New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison discovers there's more to the Kennedy assassination than the official story.

verdict.reason: Stone's maximalist conspiracy thriller demands the big screen, and this Metrograph DCP restoration brings back the visual assault that makes the three-hour runtime worthwhile. The editing, sound design, and cross-cutting between Warren Commission testimony and Garrison's investigation create a formal argument about how cinema can reshape belief.

ratings.plot: Two old pals reunite for a camping trip in Oregon's Cascade Mountains.

verdict.reason: Reichardt's most distilled film—76 minutes of genuine unease beneath stillness—plays differently on 35mm than anywhere else. The print at Metrograph restores the grain and color timing that makes the landscape feel as unsettled as the men walking through it.

ratings.plot: After experiencing tragic personal losses, a music professor rents a Seattle mansion, haunted by a slain boy.

verdict.reason: A genuinely unsettling haunted house film that earns its scares through restraint and sound design rather than gore or cheap tricks. The creaking mansion and that water tank are more effective than most horror made in the last decade.

ratings.plot: A gay cabaret owner and his drag queen companion agree to put up a false straight front so that their son can introduce them to his fiancée's right-wing, conservative parents.

verdict.reason: Nichols' timing is impeccable and the ensemble cast—Nathan Lane, Robin Williams, Gene Hackman, Dianne Wiest—lands every comedic beat without strain. The film moves at the pace of a Broadway farce, which means you'll want to catch it on a real screen where the performance energy reads.

ratings.plot: A day in the life of an unfaithful married couple and their steadily deteriorating relationship.

verdict.reason: One of Antonioni's essential works on marriage and modern alienation deserves a theatrical viewing. Metrograph's DCP restoration makes the glacial compositions and long takes hit harder than home viewing allows.

ratings.plot: In 1945, immediately following the end of Second World War, a woman who lives with her two photosensitive children on her darkened old family estate in the Channel Islands becomes convinced that the home is haunted.

verdict.reason: One of the best supernatural thrillers ever made, and Metrograph's DCP restoration gives you the chance to see Amenábar's shadows and silences the way they were designed. The twist lands harder on a big screen with an audience, and the craft—the blocking, the sound design, the slow tightening of dread—demands theatrical commitment.

ratings.plot: Two sloppy actors spend a weekend holiday at an uncle's country cottage.

verdict.reason: One of the funniest British comedies ever made—see it on the big screen where every line lands harder. Metrograph's DCP restoration sharpens the deadpan timing and gives the bleakness of 1980s London the visual weight it deserves.

ratings.plot: What did little Eve see--and how will it haunt her? Husband, father and womanizer, Louis Batiste, is the head of an affluent family, but it's the women who rule this gothic world of secrets, lies and mystic forces.

verdict.reason: A rare theatrical return for one of the finest films about family corruption and female perspective in American cinema. Lemmons' command of mood, color, and Southern Gothic atmosphere demands the scale and darkness of a theater screen.

ratings.plot: In 1938, after his father goes missing while pursuing the Holy Grail, Indiana Jones finds himself up against the Nazis again to stop them from obtaining its powers.

verdict.reason: Spielberg at his most assured—a perfect blend of action, humor, and genuine emotional weight that justifies a theatrical revisit. The father-son dynamic and Sean Connery's performance elevate this above standard adventure fare.

ratings.plot: The Platt family bands together to navigate their new surroundings after a cosmic event transports their suburban neighborhood to someplace unknown.

verdict.reason: David Robert Mitchell has earned the trust to take a big swing on theatrical format, and this cosmic displacement narrative demands the immersive scale of IMAX or 4DX to land. A 99-minute Mitchell film about suburban dislocation and family survival plays to his strengths in building dread from the intimate.

ratings.plot: Two roommates/physical therapists, one a vain woman and the other an awkward teenager, share an increasingly bizarre relationship.

verdict.reason: Altman's most cryptic and visually assured film demands the big screen—a dreamlike mystery that only deepens on repeat viewings. Metrograph's DCP restoration lets you see the pastel production design and spatial compositions that make the psychic entanglement between these women feel inevitable rather than explained.

ratings.plot: A wealthy plantation owner is captivated by a mysterious woman with a shady past.

verdict.reason: Truffaut's best film about desire and deception demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the saturated color and composed frames that make his romantic obsessions sing. The two-hour runtime clips along with real propulsion—this is pulp made by a master, not a slow study.

ratings.plot: After a car wreck on Mulholland Drive renders a woman amnesiac, she and a Hollywood-hopeful search for clues and answers across Los Angeles in a twisting venture beyond dreams and reality.

verdict.reason: One of Lynch's essential works demands the big screen, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the nocturnal Los Angeles cinematography to its intended depth. The three-hour runtime rewards full attention in a theater built for immersion.

ratings.plot: A disfigured composer sells his soul for the woman he loves so that she will perform his music, but an evil record tycoon betrays him and steals his music to open his rock palace, The Paradise.

verdict.reason: De Palma's 1974 fusion of Faust, The Phantom of the Opera, and rock opera is a formally dazzling cult film that rewards the big screen. The split-screen sequences, tracking shots, and operatic excess are built for theatrical immersion, not home viewing.

ratings.plot: A disgraced ex-policeman who runs a small ring of prostitutes finds himself in a race against time when one of his women goes missing.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's debut is a masterclass in tension and moral ambiguity that demands the big screen. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to catch the film's savage energy and grimy Seoul cinematography in theaters.

verdict.reason: The last great Showa-era kaiju spectacle and the most fun monster movie ever made. Honda and Fukuda pack 11 creatures into 88 minutes and let them trash Tokyo with anarchic joy.

verdict.reason: Tsai Ming-liang's elegiac final night in a movie palace is essential viewing on a theater's big screen. The DCP restoration at Metrograph honors both the filmmaker's precision and the cinema it mourns.

verdict.reason: Kurzel strips the play down to blood and ambition, shooting it like a brutal medieval siege rather than a costume drama. The heavy use of smoke, shadow, and handheld camera work makes the violence feel immediate and the supernatural elements genuinely unsettling on a big screen.

verdict.reason: A genuinely funny Muppet film that works for both kids and adults, with sharp comedic timing and warm heart. Brian Henson's direction keeps the pace brisk and the jokes land harder than most family movies from the '90s.

ratings.plot: A rough, short-tempered patriarch of a working-class family sees his life and the relationships around him slowly unravel.

verdict.reason: Van Sant's formal control over fragmented narrative and image—jumping timelines, Super 8 footage, elliptical editing—turns guilt into a visual experience rather than a moral lesson. Metrograph's DCP presentation locks in the deliberate haziness of the cinematography that makes the film work.

ratings.plot: Reminiscing about his dead son, a Vietnam War veteran attempts to uncover his past while suffering from a severe case of dissociation. To do so, he must decipher reality and life from his own dreams, delusions, and perceptions of ...

movies.title: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt

ratings.plot: A documentary feature about the legendary American punk band Butthole Surfers. The film tells the story of how two accounting students from Trinity College in San Antonio found solidarity in their weirdness, recruited like-minded misfits – queers, weirdos, and nonconformists like naked performance artist/dancer Kathleen Lynch – and embarked on one of the most radical rock journeys of all time. Somehow this band, with a defiantly non-commercial name, ended up as a major influence on acts like Nirvana and even scored a No. 1 hit song. Beyond the band’s story, the film tells the human story of the people behind the band. It gives an intimate look at lead singer Gibby Haynes, guitar wizard Paul Leary, drummers Teresa Nervosa and King Coffey, and bassist Jeff Pinkus – five American originals with incredible personal stories.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone who cares about American punk's weirdest and most influential act. The film captures five originals at the center of a genuinely radical career, told with the kind of intimate access that matters for a band built on refusal to compromise.

ratings.plot: Francis Ford Coppola's "A-side" to his gang war films and S.E. Hinton adaptations (with RUMBLE FISH being the "B-side") remains one of the defining films of an alternate-Brat Pack and '80s masculinity. Starring a veritable who’s who of ‘80s heroes and heartthrobs – Swayze! Cruise! Lowe! Estevez! – in some of the earliest roles of their careers. A teen gang in rural Oklahoma, the Greasers are perpetually at odds with rival group the Socs. When Greasers’ Ponyboy (C. Thomas Howell) and Johnny (Ralph Macchio) get into a brawl that ends in the accidental death of a Socs member, the boys go on the run. Soon, Ponyboy and Johnny, along with the intense Dallas (Matt Dillon) and their other Greaser buddies, must contend with the consequences of their violent lives.

verdict.reason: Coppola's definitive version of a formative '80s text deserves to be seen theatrically, especially with this cast at the peak of their early careers. The restored cut plays best on a big screen where the Oklahoma landscape and the precision of Coppola's framing actually matter.

ratings.plot: Ridley Scott making a post-apocalyptic movie is all you need to say to get us interested. THE DOG STARS swaps zombie hordes and wasteland spectacle for something quieter and more haunting: a survival story about the people who keep searching for hope after the world has already ended. Jacob Elordi leads an incredible ensemble that includes Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Allison Janney, Benedict Wong, and a grizzled-looking Guy Pearce. And yes, there is a dog in THE DOG STARS. His name is Jasper and he’s a very good boy.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic vision with Josh Brolin and Margaret Qualley deserves a big screen and an audience. The early access and ensemble cast suggest Scott is taking a genuine creative swing, not chasing spectacle.

ratings.plot: Mobilizing the full resources of the Ufa Studios, F.W. Murnau ( Nosferatu , Sunrise ) orchestrated a colossal adaptation of Goethe's FAUST that ranks alongside Fritz Lang's Metropolis as the greatest achievement of the German silent cinema. Gösta Ekman stars as the titular alchemist who, struggling with his faith amidst a devastating plague, is offered the power to cure and the gift of youth...in exchange for his soul. As the diabolical Mephisto, Emil Jannings (The Last Laugh) delivers a performance of operatic scale and intensity, by turns charming, comical, and horrific. This special Kino edition contains the Friedrich Wilhelm Murnau Foundation’s meticulous restoration of the original German version of the film (with unique hand-painted intertitles), as well as a lengthier alternate cut prepared by the Ufa Studios in 1930.

verdict.reason: Murnau's visual command and Jannings's operatic malevolence make this essential silent cinema on the big screen. The Kino restoration preserves hand-painted intertitles and gives you access to both the original German cut and the rare 1930 Ufa version in one screening.

movies.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari w/ Invincible Czars

ratings.plot: It is difficult to imagine precisely what cinema would be without its most influential and memorable titles. THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI in particular stands out as one such notable title in the international canon that in its time and forever thereafter has been heralded as a masterpiece of its craft, the singular model for expressionist, black-and-white filmmaking. A landmark of horror filmmaking, its visual style is often copied or paid homage, and its remarkable twist ending has become all but a modern trope. Its long, haunting shadows and canted, dreamlike production design stay with viewers weeks, months, and years following an initial viewing. The film is credited for introducing the "twist" ending and inspired EDWARD SCISSORHANDS by Tim Burton, THE IMAGINARIUM OF DR. PARNASSUS by Terry Gilliam, and Martin Scorsese's SHUTTER ISLAND, all of which share many striking similarities to CALIGARI. "The first thing everyone notices and best remembers about THE CABINET OF DR. CALIGARI (1920) is the film's bizarre look. The actors inhabit a jagged landscape of sharp angles and tilted walls and windows, staircases climbing crazy diagonals, trees with spiky leaves, grass that looks like knives. These radical distortions immediately set the film apart from all earlier ones." – Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

verdict.reason: Watch it. A 1920 expressionist landmark that shaped everything that followed, and live music transforms a silent masterpiece into an event.

ratings.plot: In the town of Wisbourg, estate agent Mr. Knock is pleased to receive a commission from Count Orlok to find a house for him. He dispatches his young assistant, Hutter, to Orlok's castle in the far-off Carpathians. He tells Hutter to get him to buy the vacant house just opposite Hutter's own. Hutter arrives at his destination safely and the Count is all too eager to buy the proposed property, especially after he sees a photo of Hutter's pretty young wife Ellen. Hutter soon realizes the evil he's dealing with and is locked away while Orlock makes his way by ship to Wisbourg. As Orlok travels to Wisbourg, plague descends in his wake and the people of Wisbourg begin to sense the coming of evil. Hutter eventually escapes Orlok's castle, determined to return home as quickly as possible, but exhausted and ill, finds himself in hospital. Hutter nonetheless arrives home the same day as Orlok and the townsfolk begin to panic over the increasing number of deaths.

verdict.reason: See this foundational vampire film on the big screen with a live band that earned its reputation by understanding silent cinema's rhythmic hunger. Murnau's visual architecture—shadows as living things, composition as dread—demands theatrical space and the Invincible Czars provide the pulse that transforms viewing into ritual.

ratings.plot: In a post-apocalyptic world, a virus wipes out humanity. Survivors face roaming scavengers called Reapers. Protagonist Hig, a pilot, survived the flu but lost his wife.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's post-apocalyptic adaptation arrives untested and unreleased elsewhere, making this a risky $18 bet on a filmmaker whose recent output has been uneven. A two-hour survival slog about grief and isolation is better experienced at home where you can pause it.

ratings.plot: Heroes from three different worlds must unite when they're thrust together to confront a catastrophic danger that could destroy everything they know.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Marvel's formula has run thin and 165 minutes of multiverse fan service doesn't justify a theatrical trip. The Russo Brothers are reliably competent but have nothing new to say about superhero spectacle.

ratings.plot: Gemma, a young mother raising her daughter in the house she grew up in, discovers she can travel into The Further, where she possesses an ability to bring what lives there back to the real world.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the Insidious franchise has exhausted its premise, and a sixth entry with a new director lacks any reason to leave the couch tonight. The plot gimmick of bringing entities back from The Further is the same haunted-house-next-door problem the series has recycled since 2010.

movies.title: The Rivals of Amziah King Cocktail Party Screening

ratings.plot: Some people steal cash. Some steal cars. In THE RIVALS OF AMZIAH KING, they're stealing bees. Matthew McConaughey stars as a charismatic Oklahoma beekeeper, bluegrass bandleader, and local legend whose thriving honey operation puts a target on his back. When his estranged foster daughter returns, he sees a chance to build something lasting together. But in the surprisingly cutthroat world of commercial honey, jealous rivals (including Kurt Russell) are ready to sting first.

verdict.reason: A gimmick premise about bee theft does not carry a 130-minute film, and McConaughey's charm cannot fix the thin setup. The cocktail-party format at Alamo Drafthouse invites distraction, which this script cannot afford.

ratings.plot: After a drug-fueled car crash, ex-private schoolboys Ayden and Jesse escape into the Melbourne CBD and are plunged into a night of unbridled debauchery and rapidly escalating violence.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the film squanders a solid premise with sloppy execution and self-indulgent direction that mistakes chaos for consequence. At 93 minutes it still feels bloated, and Aroni's style prioritizes surface-level provocation over any genuine insight into his characters or their spiral.

ratings.plot: A bullied girl transfers schools hoping for peace, but her past trauma isolates her-until she discovers a series of secret letters hidden around the school, leading her on a mysterious quest to uncover their sender's true intent.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the animation and premise don't justify a theater trip when the emotional beats land better in quieter formats. A 96-minute anime about isolation and mystery works harder in isolation than in a multiplex full of distractions.

ratings.plot: In a small Texas town where high school football looms large, coach Eric Taylor leads through wins and losses both on and off the field.

verdict.reason: This is a TV series, not a theatrical film — streaming or home viewing is the natural habitat for episodic television. A 97-minute runtime suggests a single episode or clip package, which defeats the point of the show's strength as a season-long narrative.

ratings.plot: Two-time GRAMMY®-nominated global girl group KATSEYE is coming to cinemas worldwide with a special theatrical release ahead of their third EP, WILD . KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS is a captivating journey into the group's bold new era while celebrating the fans who helped make it possible. Featuring never-before-seen footage, EYEKONS fan videos, and intimate interviews from the group members, the film explores the powerful bond between KATSEYE and their global fandom. A love letter to the EYEKONS who helped build this movement, KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS reveals why this group's story is only just beginning. From the intense pressure of Dream Academy to chart-topping viral success, audiences experience the highs, setbacks, sacrifices, and breakthrough moments that transformed KATSEYE on their path to global pop stardom. Praised by outlets including The New York Times , Vogue , Rolling Stone , and Billboard , KATSEYE has earned acclaim for their relentless dedication to their craft and electrifying live performances. As one of pop's most exciting emerging global acts, the group continues to solidify its place as a worldwide force. From the same team that created Netflix’s POP STAR ACADEMY, KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS is produced by Interscope Films and Boardwalk Pictures, in partnership with HYBE X GEFFEN, and directed by Nadia Hallgren.

verdict.reason: A 80-minute promotional film masquerading as documentary has no theatrical urgency when the same material will land on a streamer within weeks. Nadia Hallgren's direction here amounts to polished marketing for an EP release, not cinema.

ratings.plot: After his billionaire industrialist boss is murdered in front of him, Cole Reed is set up to take the fall for the crime -- leaving him on the run as he works to uncover an international conspiracy.

verdict.reason: Skip it; a 95-minute thriller about framing and conspiracy is standard studio fare that will play better on streaming than in a theater. Jean-François Richet made solid action work years ago, but this setup belongs on a Tuesday night at home, not on a night out.

ratings.plot: An ex-military man working at a Georgia power plant has to spring into action to prevent disaster when a group of rogue soldiers gain control of the plant and take the employees hostage.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a routine action thriller with no theatrical urgency or artistic distinction. The 97-minute runtime and direct-to-streaming DNA make it better suited to home viewing than a trip to the cinema.

ratings.plot: Elijah Peel, a rock star engulfed in addiction and self-destruction, confronts his past after a heart attack. Meeting a wise, terminally ill girl, he seeks redemption, facing painful sacrifices to save his life and soul.

verdict.reason: Skip it; a 2026 release date and missing director/runtime data suggest this is either unreleased or fabricated, and the redemption-through-illness premise trades in worn recovery narrative beats. Without a completed film, a known filmmaker, or theatrical urgency, there is nothing to recommend tonight.

ratings.plot: A mute gunfighter defends a young widow and a group of outlaws against a gang of bounty killers in the winter of 1898, and a grim, tense struggle unfolds.

Friends on a late-night food run become trapped on an infinite highway with otherworldly terrors lurking beyond. Confined in their Jeep Cherokee, they must decide whether to accept their fate or attempt escape.

verdict.reason: A debut feature with an intriguing premise and committed execution, but the 89-minute runtime and confined setting work better as a short form idea than a full narrative arc. The IFC Center screening is the right venue for experimental genre work, though wait for word-of-mouth before committing.

ratings.plot: A psychopath tries to forcibly persuade a tennis star to agree to his theory that two strangers can get away with murder by submitting to his plan to kill the other's most-hated person.
After a bad gambling bet, a schoolteacher is marooned in a town full of crazy, drunk, violent men who threaten to make him just as crazy, drunk, and violent.

A girl with few real prospects joins a gang, reinventing herself and gaining a sense of self confidence in the process. However, she soon finds that this new life does not necessarily make her any happier.
A devout Catholic man's rigid principles are challenged during a one-night stay with Maud, a divorced woman with an outsize personality.

Acclaimed conductor Thibaut has leukemia and needs a bone marrow donor. Learning he was adopted, he finds an older brother, a musician and factory worker. Their reunion sparks a fraternal, musical journey amidst the town's factory...
Assigned to a county-mandated drug court program, Cody Parsons embarks on the tenuous journey toward recovery amidst the opioid epidemic in rural Ohio.

verdict.reason: A strong independent film, but IFC Center is the only NYC venue and the runtime will determine whether this is a theater trip or a home watch. Check the length before committing.

ratings.plot: After Clive Randolph finally returns home from Gold Coast colony, younger brother John balks at following the family Colonial Service tradition. But back in Gold Coast, one Zurof, nominally studying ants, pursues a hidden politica...

verdict.reason: A handsome 1939 studio picture with real craft, but the colonial adventure plot feels thin and the runtime asks patience for modest rewards. The IFC Center screening is the right venue for a restored print, though the film works just as well at home.

ratings.plot: Elliot lands a job for Erika Tracy as her sexual muse.

verdict.reason: Gregg Araki working in comedy-drama territory is worth an evening, but ninety minutes at BAM or Alamo Drafthouse is a low-stakes gamble rather than a must-see. The premise is thin enough that execution matters more than premise, and without special format or restoration hook, this lands as a solid rental candidate that happens to be screening now.

ratings.plot: It's Girl Scout Cookie season, and four tenacious girls strive to be a top-selling "Cookie Queen," navigating an $800 million business in which innocence and ambition collide.
A group of Yokohama teens look to save their school's clubhouse from the wrecking ball in preparations for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics.
A food influencer secretly struggles with bulimia as she navigates online fame, close friendships, and a painful past.

A modern family relocates to the countryside where the children discover a magical tree with eccentric residents. They're transported to fantastical lands, rekindling their family bond through adventures.

verdict.reason: A solidly crafted family adventure with genuine warmth, but the 110-minute runtime drags in the middle and the fantastical set pieces don't quite justify a theatrical trip over waiting for home viewing. Ben Gregor stages the tree-world sequences with real invention, yet the film never builds to anything that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: A reclusive retired professor is faced with confronting modernity when a group of vulgar youths led by an obnoxious marchesa take up residence in his unused upper residence.
A middle-aged playboy becomes fascinated by the daughter of a private detective who has been hired to entrap him with the wife of a client.

In a French seaside town, at a boarding house for civil servants recovering from surgery and maladies, the six male residents' lives change dramatically when two women arrive: Catherine, lively, sexually liberated, willing to kiss...

verdict.reason: Jacques Brel's only film is a curious artifact of 1970s European cinema with genuine warmth, but the 91 minutes sag under thin plotting and uneven tonal control. Lincoln Center's screening makes it worth considering if you're already exploring the venue's calendar, though it plays better as a historical footnote than as a living work.

ratings.plot: Three buddies drive cross-country in a van, causing mayhem and mischief while racing to LA for their big break: opening for Green Day on New Year's Eve.

verdict.reason: Without director, runtime, or venue context, the call rests on execution quality alone, and multiplex chains offer no theatrical advantage over home viewing. Check the runtime before committing—if it's under 90 minutes, it's worth a matinee; anything longer demands stronger justification.

ratings.plot: A criminal psychologist who turned agoraphobic after a murder attempt agrees to help two San Francisco detectives hunt for a copycat serial killer who intends on making her his next victim.

verdict.reason: A sharp 90s thriller with real tension between Sigourney Weaver's agoraphobic psychologist and the serial killer hunting her, but the runtime drags and the third act relies on plot mechanics rather than character. The theatrical experience matters here—Weaver's claustrophobia plays better on a big screen than at home.

movies.title: Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass

ratings.plot: When her fiancé uses their "celebrity pass" agreement, Midwest bride Gail Daughtry travels to Hollywood seeking revenge by pursuing her own celebrity encounter.

verdict.reason: David Wain's timing and ensemble instinct can elevate broad premise comedy, but this one rides a single joke for 93 minutes. The Alamo Drafthouse is the right venue for a crowd-pleaser that needs noise and company to land.

ratings.plot: In Finnish forest, Saga and her husband Jon embark on a new chapter as parents. But Saga's joy is overshadowed by a chilling suspicion about their newborn, unbeknownst to Jon, causing a rift as she alone grapples with the disturbi...
Two rock-bottom drivers transport a wealthy teen to rehab, but their simple job spirals into a chaotic journey of drugs, danger, and crime as their passenger derails their plans.

verdict.reason: Macon Blair's direction of a crime-comedy premise has promise, but the 98-minute runtime and uneven execution suggest this works better as a late-night streaming watch than a theater trip. The Alamo Drafthouse is the right venue if you want the full rowdy experience, but the film itself doesn't demand the big screen.

ratings.plot: When a couple decides to adopt a stray cat their perspective on life changes radically, literally altering the course of time and space and testing their faith in each other and themselves.

verdict.reason: Miranda July's strangest film has real formal inventiveness but uneven execution and a runtime that outlasts its premise. Anthology's DCP presentation is clean, though this particular work benefits more from home viewing's pause button than theatrical immersion.

ratings.plot: President Reagan races to save a nuclear deal with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev as pressure mounts all around him. Every word spoken could move the world closer to peace - or destruction.

verdict.reason: A competent political thriller with genuine stakes, but the runtime tests patience and the theatrical experience doesn't justify the multiplex ticket over waiting for home viewing. Michael Russell Gunn stages the Reagan-Gorbachev negotiations with workmanlike tension, though nothing here demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: Professor Se Jeong attends a biotech conference, only to witness it spiral into catastrophe when a rapidly mutating virus is unleashed. As the outbreak spreads and the infected begin to transform, authorities seal off the entire f...

verdict.reason: Yeon Sang-ho brings kinetic action chops to a virus-outbreak premise, but the film splits focus between spectacle and coherence in ways that undercut both. The set pieces have real visceral impact on a theater screen, which is the only reason to show up.

ratings.plot: The life and death of "Dracula" writer Bram Stoker is discussed, as well as the themes of the novel and several film adaptations of "Dracula," and the cultural impact of the work. While critics of the time were not receptive to th...

verdict.reason: A compact documentary on Stoker's life and Dracula's cultural reach, worth an hour at Metrograph if you're curious about the novel's origins and film legacy. The DCP presentation is clean, but fifty-six minutes of talking heads and adaptation clips works just as well at home.

ratings.plot: In the summer of 1962, a new kid in town is taken under the wing of a young baseball prodigy and his rowdy team, resulting in many adventures.

verdict.reason: A nostalgia play that works best as a communal summer night out, not as a film that holds up to scrutiny. The 101-minute runtime is lean enough for a casual theater visit, but the script trades on sentiment rather than genuine humor or drama.

ratings.plot: Grossly overweight yet good-hearted professor Sherman Klump takes a special chemical that turns him into the slim but obnoxious Buddy Love.

verdict.reason: Eddie Murphy's dual performance carries a middling comedy that works best as comfort viewing rather than a theater event. The 95-minute runtime and broad slapstick hold up better on a couch than in a packed multiplex.

ratings.plot: Single mother Vianne Rocher and her young daughter arrive in a rural French town in the winter of 1959, and open an unusual chocolate shop that disrupts the moral fiber of the strictly Catholic townsfolk and mayor.
The Autobots must stop a colossal planet-consuming robot who goes after the Autobot Matrix of Leadership. At the same time, they must defend themselves against an all-out attack from the Decepticons.

verdict.reason: Skip unless you're seeing it at Alamo Drafthouse for the theatrical experience and nostalgia factor. The 1986 animated film is a cult object that plays better as a communal event than alone, and at 84 minutes it's slight enough for a night out without demanding much.

ratings.plot: Events over the course of one traumatic night in Paris unfold in reverse-chronological order.

verdict.reason: Only worth the trip if you can handle Noé's most punishing work without walking out. The reverse chronology structure and 13-minute single-take rape scene make this an endurance test that demands big-screen commitment.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: John Woo's first English-language film in years has genuine craft moments, but the execution is uneven and the premise wears thin before the final act. The Lincoln Center booking is respectable, but this is a minor entry from a major director—worth catching only if you're committed to tracking his recent work.

ratings.plot: An escort who caters to Washington, D.C.'s society ladies becomes involved in a murder case.

verdict.reason: Schrader's pulp thriller misfires in execution, but Anthology's DCP restoration gives a minor work its best possible presentation. The film is worth catching only if you're tracking the director's output or need to see it on a proper screen tonight.

ratings.plot: Armed men hijack a New York City subway train, holding the passengers hostage in return for a ransom, and turning an ordinary day's work for dispatcher Walter Garber into a face-off with the mastermind behind the crime.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's hyperkinetic style clashes with a rote hostage thriller, but the 35mm print at Film Forum restores visual snap that streaming erases. The subway setting and Denzel-John Travolta pairing warrant a big screen if you're in the mood for slick procedural noise.

ratings.plot: A classic tale about bitter relationships between a frivolous girl and a soldier is adapted for the post-World War II time.

verdict.reason: Clouzot's adaptation has genuine power but arrives uneven and padded at 100 minutes. The Film at Lincoln Center restoration makes this the only way to see it properly on a big screen, and the post-war Paris setting carries real historical weight if you're willing to sit with the film's tonal shifts.

ratings.plot: Two gunfighters separate and experience surreal visions on their journey through the west.

verdict.reason: A weird 1971 musical-western hybrid with real charm and strangeness, but the film is uneven and works best as a curiosity. Anthology's 35mm print makes it worth the trip if you're in the mood for oddball Americana and don't mind sitting through 93 minutes of trippy excess.

ratings.plot: The wife of a university research scientist believes that her lakeside Vermont home is haunted by a ghost - or that she is losing her mind.

verdict.reason: Zemeckis's craft elevates a thin supernatural mystery into something watchable, but the 130-minute runtime drags a third-act twist that doesn't earn its setup. The 35mm print at Metrograph is the only reason to see it in a theater instead of streaming.

ratings.plot: Living in exile, Dr. Hannibal Lecter tries to reconnect with now disgraced F.B.I. Agent Clarice Starling, and finds himself a target of revenge from a powerful victim.

verdict.reason: Ridley Scott's baroque excess and 35mm presentation at Metrograph salvage a sequel that collapses under its own ambition. The runtime bloats a thin premise, but the visual design and Scott's commitment to style over substance reward patient viewers on the big screen.

ratings.plot: An aspiring actress disappointed by her treatment in the movie industry turns to phone sex to make a living.

verdict.reason: Spike Lee misfires on satire about exploitation in Hollywood and the sex industry, but the film has enough visual wit and Barbara Nunn's performance to justify a trip if you're tracking his uneven 90s work. The theatrical format lets you catch Lee's signature style even when the material doesn't land.

ratings.plot: In 2017, a successful businessman travels to the ends of the earth to find that the perfect woman is always under his nose. He hires a sexy renegade tracker to find an exact duplicate of his android wife.

verdict.reason: A dopey 80s sex-bot romp with genuine charm and a game cast, but the premise outstays its welcome well before the ninety-minute mark. The Alamo Drafthouse is the right venue for this kind of cult obscurity if you're in the mood for something deliberately silly.

ratings.plot: Live-action adaptation of the 2016 Disney animated film 'Moana.'

Apartment building superintendent Cleveland Heep rescues what he thinks is a young woman from the pool he maintains. When he discovers that she is actually a character from a bedtime story who is trying to make the journey back to...

verdict.reason: Shyamalan's strangest work has cult defenders, and the 35mm print at Metrograph makes it worth seeing if you're game for failure dressed up as ambition. The theatrical experience rescues nothing, but the film's delusional conviction about its own mythology is at least committed enough to deserve a big screen.

movies.title: A Day in the Country + People on Sunday
My Heart Is That Eternal Rose

ratings.plot: Two lovers are willing to do anything to reunite after criminals separate them.

verdict.reason: Patrick Tam's 1989 Hong Kong crime drama deserves a look on the big screen, but the 90-minute runtime and modest reputation mean it works just as well at home. Metrograph's DCP presentation of an obscure 35-year-old title suggests this is a restoration worth catching if you're already in the neighborhood.

movies.title: PRIVATE EVENT TODAY IN THEATER & COMMISSARY
Saturday Afternoon Cartoons: Bugs We Love(?)

ratings.plot: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you need 70 minutes of curated cat content on a big screen with an audience. The appeal lives entirely in the curation and communal laughter, which works at IFC Center but streams fine at home.

movies.title: Freefall: A Reckoning for Boeing (Open Captioning)

ratings.plot: An underdog American team competes for first place at France's Mondial du Fromage: the Olympics of cheese.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're in the mood for a light competition doc that plays like a sports movie about cheese. The premise is charming but the theatrical experience doesn't offer much that streaming won't deliver just as well from your couch.

ratings.plot: In the late 21st century, an investigator and a member of a feared religious sect are brought together by a murder in a refugee camp.

Former competitive runner turned photographer Aisha McAdams documents elite ultra marathon athletes. After trauma forced her from the sport, she wonders if she can find her way back by entering an ultra-marathon herself.
Tells the story of the six wives of Henry VIII, reimagining them as pop stars who reclaim their narratives from their infamous husband's shadow.

verdict.reason: The stage show works because of its raw energy and live performance; a filmed version loses that immediacy and becomes a recording of something better experienced in a theater. The 95-minute runtime suggests heavy editing that may have flattened the songs' impact.

ratings.plot: Three friends in their mid-thirties as they road trip across the Midwestern United States in search of their friend who has seemingly disappeared off the grid.

Inspired by a best selling true story by Sharon Yitzhaki. Sharon went to Bolivia with a young guy she barely knew. She was framed and accused of smuggling 10 kilos of cocaine across the border. They threw her into Bolivia's most a...

Big Shark with Tommy Wiseau In Person

ratings.plot: Classical Period is a portrait of Cal and his friends in Philadelphia. They meet and have long conversations about books, poetry, music, and architecture, most notably Henry Longfellow's 1864 translation of Dante's Divine Comedy ....

verdict.reason: A 62-minute film of conversation about books and poetry has genuine charm, but it asks a lot of patience for modest rewards. Fendt's quiet naturalism works best on a smaller screen where you control the pacing.

verdict.reason: A three-hour opera film demands commitment, but Metge's take on Mozart's comedy has real wit if you're in the mood for theatrical excess. The Lincoln Center screening gives you the proper scale, though streaming at home won't punish you much.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to three hours of Puccini opera in a theatrical setting. The 1991 staging prioritizes sung drama over spectacle, which works best on a cinema screen with pristine sound.

ratings.plot: Richard Wagner's last opera has remained controversial since its first performance for its unique, and, for some, unsavory blending of religious and erotic themes and imagery. Based on one of the medieval epic romances of King Art...

verdict.reason: Syberberg's four-hour operatic vision is uncompromising and visually baroque, but demands absolute commitment and tolerance for his deliberately confrontational staging of Wagner's final work. The theatrical experience is singular, though patience and appetite for avant-garde opera aesthetics are prerequisites.

ratings.plot: While the rest of the Hebrews bewail their fate, Samson alone trusts in God's promise of liberty. Abimelech, the Philistine satrap of Gaza, enters to mock the Hebrews' God, proclaiming the superiority of Dagon, and the Hebrews are...

verdict.reason: A filmed opera from a 1981 production—worthwhile if you want grand vocal performance on a big screen, but the two-hour runtime and static staging make this better suited to home viewing with a pause button. Browning's direction prioritizes the singers over cinematic language, so you're essentially watching a stage performance captured in a theater.

ratings.plot: After a terrible car accident, a man makes sure his wife dies as a result in order to get her inheritance, and will commit sabotage and murder so he can't get blamed for her death.

verdict.reason: A obscure 1975 crime film with a genuinely nasty premise deserves a look if you're hunting for forgotten genre work, but the execution is thin and the runtime doesn't justify the one-note revenge setup. Film at Lincoln Center is the right venue for a restoration gamble, but proceed only if you've exhausted the obvious repertory titles.
